title: The QMD File
text: A .qmd file is a plain text file combining Markdown for prose and code chunks for computation. This chapter covers the options that give you precise control over how code runs and how content is shown.

title: The QMD File
text:
Code chunk options
By default, Quarto shows both the code and its output. Chunk options let you change this: hiding code in a final report, adding captions, or skipping slow computations, without touching the code itself.
Every option is written as a #| comment at the top of the chunk. The chunk below runs print("Hello!") but hides the source code and suppresses warnings:
```{.python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| output: true
#| warning: false
print("Hello!")
```






NoteWhy {.python} instead of {python}?



Curly braces without a dot, {python}, tell Quarto to execute that block as Python code. This is what you want in your actual document, but in a tutorial like this one we only want to show the syntax.
Adding a dot, {.python}, switches the block to display-only: Quarto still applies Python syntax highlighting, but never runs the code. Alternatively, wrapping the entire example in a four-backtick ````markdown fence achieves the same effect.
In your own .qmd files, use {python} (no dot) so the chunk actually runs.



Option reference








Option
Values
What it controls




echo
true / false / fenced
Show the source code


eval
true / false
Actually run the code


output
true / false / asis
Show the output


warning
true / false
Show warnings


error
true / false
Show errors (instead of stopping)


include
true / false
false: the code runs, but neither code nor output appears


code-fold
true / false
Collapse code into a toggle


code-summary
string
Label for the fold toggle


fig-cap
string
Caption for figures


fig-align
left / center / right
Figure alignment


label
string
ID of the chunk. For cross-referencing it must start with fig- or tbl-





Common combinations
These three patterns cover most everyday use cases:


Hide code, show output
#| echo: false
The code runs silently and readers see only the result. Ideal for polished reports.

Show code, don’t run
#| eval: false
Useful for illustrative examples or code that would fail in the current environment.

Collapsible code block
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
Keeps the page clean while still letting curious readers expand the source.

title: The QMD File
text:
Global chunk defaults
Repeating the same options on every single chunk is tedious and error-prone. Set defaults once in _quarto.yml. They apply to every chunk in the project, and you only override where needed:


_quarto.yml

execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false

title: The QMD File
text:
Conditional content
Sometimes you need different text for different audiences or output formats: a simplified explanation for beginners and extra detail for advanced readers, or an interactive widget in HTML that does not exist in PDF.

Profile-based content
Profiles are defined in _quarto.yml. Quarto evaluates them at render time; the .qmd source stays the same for every audience.


Markdown
::: {.content-visible when-profile="english"}
This paragraph only appears in the English build.
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-profile="beg"}
Hidden in the beg profile, visible everywhere else.
:::

What happens
quarto render --profile english includes the blocks tagged when-profile="english". Blocks tagged when-profile="deutsch" are dropped.
This is how the pages of this tutorial are built: every file contains one block per language.




Format-based content


Markdown
::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
This only appears in HTML output.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
This only appears in PDF output.
:::

What happens
Quarto checks the output format at render time. Only the matching block is included; the rest is silently dropped.
Use this to embed interactive HTML elements while providing a static alternative for PDF.

title: The QMD File
text:
Cross-referencing
Cross-references let you write @fig-sine in prose and have Quarto automatically produce “Figure 1”, with a hyperlink in HTML and the correct number even if figures are reordered.

Figures


Markdown
```{.python}
#| label: fig-sine
#| fig-cap: "A plot of sin(x)"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
x = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 200)
plt.plot(x, np.sin(x))
plt.show()
```

As shown in @fig-sine, the sine function...

What happens
The label option registers the figure; fig-cap sets the caption. Writing @fig-sine in prose becomes a clickable “Figure 1” link in HTML and the correct number in PDF. Quarto handles the counting.
Labels for figures must start with fig-.








Note



Reminder: Use {python} instead of {.python} in your own document. The dot version is only used here to prevent execution in this tutorial.




Tables


Markdown
```{.python}
#| label: tbl-data
#| tbl-cap: "Summary statistics"
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1,2,3], "y": [4,5,6]})
df
```

The values in @tbl-data show...

What happens
Works the same as figures: @tbl-data becomes “Table 1” wherever you write it. Labels for tables must start with tbl-.




Sections


Markdown
## Introduction {#sec-intro}

As described in @sec-intro...

What happens
Adding {#sec-intro} to any heading makes it referenceable. @sec-intro becomes “Section 1” with a link if sections are numbered (number-sections: true). Section labels must start with sec-.








TipLabel naming rules




Figure labels must start with fig-
Table labels must start with tbl-
Section labels must start with sec-

title: The QMD File
text:
Custom divs and spans
CSS classes applied to a block let you style content directly from the .qmd file. Quarto passes the class straight through to the HTML output.


Markdown
::: {.my-class}
This block gets the `my-class` CSS class.
:::
For inline styling, use a span:
This word is [highlighted]{.my-highlight} in the text.

Output

This block gets the my-class CSS class.

This word is highlighted in the text.



Built-in Bootstrap utility classes
These work out of the box without any custom CSS:



Class
Effect




.text-center
Centre-align text


.text-muted
Grey text


.fw-bold
Bold text


.border
Add a border


.bg-light
Light background


.p-3
Add padding


.mt-4
Add top margin





Markdown
::: {.border .p-3 .bg-light}
This box has a border, padding, and a light background, with no custom CSS.
:::

Output

This box has a border, padding, and a light background, with no custom CSS.

title: The QMD File
text:
Callout blocks
Callouts draw attention to important information without breaking the flow of the text. Quarto renders them as styled boxes with an icon. Use them for tips, warnings, or critical notes.


Markdown
::: {.callout-note}
## Optional title
Informational note.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
Practical advice.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
Something to watch out for.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
Critical information.
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
Proceed carefully.
:::

Output






NoteOptional title



Informational note.








Tip



Practical advice.








Warning



Something to watch out for.








Important



Critical information.








Caution



Proceed carefully.




Add collapse="true" to make a callout collapsible. Readers expand it on demand:


Markdown
::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Click to expand
Hidden detail.
:::

Output






NoteClick to expand





Hidden detail.

title: Extensions
text:
This chapter covers the extensions used in this tutorial. An extension is installed once per project with quarto add <name>. The files land in _extensions/ and should be committed to git.
Extensions can be enabled globally in _quarto.yml or per page in the header of the file:

title: Extensions
text:
quizdown — interactive quizzes
Install: quarto add parmsam/quizdown Source: (Sauer 2023), github.com/parmsam/quarto-quizdown

---
locale: en
---

# Which file controls global project settings in Quarto?

1. [x] `_quarto.yml`
1. [ ] `index.qmd`
1. [ ] `styles.css`

# Select all valid Quarto output formats.

- [x] HTML
- [x] PDF
- [x] Word (.docx)
- [ ] Excel (.xlsx)

# Put the Quarto render pipeline in the correct order.

1. Parse `.qmd` source
2. Execute code chunks
3. Convert Markdown to HTML/PDF
4. Apply theme and styles


SettingsQuestion typesImages & code


Global quiz settings go inside a --- block at the top of the quiz:
```{quizdown}
---
shuffleAnswers: true    # default: true — randomise answer order
shuffleQuestions: false # default: false — randomise question order
locale: en              # language of the buttons
---
```






Tip



shuffleAnswers: true is the default. Answers are shuffled unless you explicitly set it to false.




Single choice, exactly one correct answer:
```{quizdown}
# What is 2 + 2?
1. [ ] 3
1. [x] 4
1. [ ] 5
```
Multiple choice, more than one correct answer:
```{quizdown}
# Which of these are programming languages?
- [x] Python
- [ ] Quarto
- [x] R
- [x] JavaScript
```
Ordering, the items have to be sorted:
```{quizdown}
# Put the Quarto render pipeline in the correct order.

1. Parse `.qmd` source
2. Execute code chunks
3. Convert Markdown to HTML/PDF
4. Apply theme and styles
```


Include an image in a question:
```{quizdown}
# What does this logo belong to?
![](https://quarto.org/quarto.png)
1. [x] Quarto
1. [ ] RMarkdown
```
Include inline code in answers:
```{quizdown}
# Which chunk option hides the source code?
1. [x] `echo: false`
1. [ ] `eval: false`
1. [ ] `output: false`
```

title: Extensions
section: pyodide-interaktiv — live Python in the browser
text:
pyodide-interaktiv — live Python in the browser
Install: quarto add Erasmus-CTM/pyodide-interaktiv Source: (Erasmus CTM, n.d.c), github.com/Erasmus-CTM/pyodide-interaktiv. The Python behind it is Pyodide (Droettboom et al. 2021).
pyodide-interaktiv runs Python in a Web Worker, that is next to the page rather than inside it. The page therefore stays usable during a long computation, and every cell has a Stop button. The extension is a rework of coatless-quarto/pyodide.

ExampleShared stateinput()Plots & animationAI feedbackOptionsMarker cellsLimits



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Every cell offers Run code (also Shift + Enter), Reset, Copy, Feedback and + Code block. The last one appends an empty, editable cell, handy under a read-only example.




{python}
{pyodide-python}




Runs at
Render time
Read time (in the browser)


Reader can edit
No
Yes


Needs Python installed
Yes (author)
No


Output baked into HTML
Yes
No, computed live









WarningPackage availability



Pyodide runs in WebAssembly. Many packages are available (numpy, pandas, matplotlib, sympy), but not every package with C extensions is.




All cells on a page share one Python session. A later cell can use anything an earlier one defined, once the earlier one has been run:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Running the lower cell first gives a NameError. So tell your readers to run the cells from top to bottom.
Cells that should run before the reader touches anything use context: setup. Cells whose result is shown but whose code is hidden use context: output.






Notepy-exercise does not see these variables



An exercise from py-exercise runs in its own, empty namespace. Whatever was defined in a {pyodide-python} cell does not exist there. Everything the exercise needs has to be inside the exercise itself.




A cell can stop and wait for typed input without freezing the page:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Warninginput() needs cross-origin isolation



Blocking input relies on SharedArrayBuffer, which browsers only hand out to cross-origin-isolated pages. A service worker shipped with the extension sets the required headers automatically on your own domain. Learning platforms such as Moodle usually block service workers. There input() is unavailable and the page says so. Everything else keeps working.




Code behaves like on your own computer: plt.show() triggers the output. Without the call nothing appears. A static plot is shown as an image first and then replaced by an interactive view with a toolbar (zoom, pan, reset, save). If that fails, the image stays.
An animation needs no extra call:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
A live version of this is on the Visualizations page of the Example Page.






TipSpeed is interval, not frames



interval is the delay between frames in milliseconds; 33 ms is roughly 30 frames per second. Matplotlib’s default of 200 ms looks visibly choppy. frames only sets how many frames are drawn, so raising it makes the animation longer, not smoother. Every frame is pre-rendered and embedded, so long animations cost computing time.


For special cases, zeige_animation(ani, format="gif") and zeige_animation(ani, fps=30) control format and frame rate directly.


Every interactive cell has a Feedback button that sends the current code plus its output to a language model and shows the answer under the cell. The ⚙ icon at the top of the document opens the settings:







Field
Meaning




Provider preset
fills in base URL and an example model for OpenRouter, Cerebras, Groq, OpenAI or Ollama


Base URL
API endpoint, e.g. https://openrouter.ai/api/v1


API key
stays in the browser, never in the rendered page


Model
free text. Fetch models lists the provider’s models, free ones only by default


Feedback mode
Direct API or Copy prompt


Storage
localStorage (persistent) or sessionStorage (per tab)



Without an API key, Copy prompt mode produces a ready-to-paste text for ChatGPT, Claude and the like.
Hints get more concrete with each click on the same cell. There are three levels: 1 = gentle nudge, 2 = names the problem, 3 = describes the solution approach in words. Finished solution code is never given. Turn it off with feedback-hints: false.


page.qmd

pyodide:
  feedback: true            # show Feedback buttons (default: true)
  feedback-storage: local   # local | session
  feedback-hints: true      # progressive hints (default: true)







Important



The API key lives in the reader’s browser. Never put a key into the .qmd; it would be published with the site.




Per cell:








Option
Default
Description




context
interactive
interactive, output or setup


read-only
false
editor is locked (no Feedback button)


autorun
—
true: runs by itself once Pyodide has started


code-fold
—
true: cell starts collapsed, false: expanded. Falls back to the document’s code-fold: when unset


pdf-fallback
—
true: in PDF, Word etc. the cell appears as ordinary, highlighted Python code


<format>-autoexec
—
true: for that one format (e.g. pdf-autoexec) the cell is actually run at render time and its output shown


label
—
unique cell ID


classes
—
extra CSS classes


fig-cap
—
caption for plots


fig-width / fig-height
7 / 5
plot size in inches



Per document:


page.qmd

pyodide:
  packages: [numpy, pandas]   # installed at startup via micropip
  show-startup-message: true
  pdf-fallback: false         # PDF/Word: show cells as Python code
  pdf-autoexec: false         # PDF: run cells at render time
  lang: de                    # interface language (default: en)

Packages that only appear in an import are fetched on demand, so packages: is for the ones you want ready before the first run. requests and urllib3 are shimmed, so pd.read_csv(url) works.
The interface language comes from Quarto’s own lang:. Shipped are en, de, sv, no/nb and da. A multilingual project therefore needs no extra setting, see Multilanguage Projects.
code-fold: is Quarto’s ordinary option. With code-tools: true, the page’s “Show All Code” toggle folds and unfolds the Pyodide cells too. <format>-autoexec needs a Python installation on the machine that renders.


A figure from a {pyodide-python} cell cannot be cross-referenced with @fig-.... If you need a numbered, linkable figure, write a normal {python} cell and make it interactive in HTML with a # pyodide: ... comment:
```{python}
#| label: fig-parabola
#| fig-cap: "The parabola $y=x^2$."
# pyodide: autorun, read-only=false
x = np.linspace(-2, 2, 200)
plt.plot(x, x**2)
plt.show()
```
The marker takes the same options as the table in the “Options” tab and is removed from the displayed code. PDF and Word keep Quarto’s real figure. In HTML the interactive cell takes its place, while caption and cross-reference target stay. The cell needs a real Python at render time, like any {python} cell.



Stop: On cross-origin-isolated pages, Stop aborts gracefully and the variables survive. Otherwise Stop restarts Python, the variables are lost, and setup, output and autorun cells run again by themselves.
Only one cell can compute at a time.
Navigating to another page of the project reloads Python.
embed-resources: true gives a single working file, but not one that works offline: Pyodide itself is still fetched from the network. The file has to be served over http(s); double-clicking the local file is not enough.

title: Extensions
section: py-exercise — editable exercises with hidden tests
text:
py-exercise — editable exercises with hidden tests
Install: quarto add Erasmus-CTM/py-exercise Source: (Erasmus CTM, n.d.b), github.com/Erasmus-CTM/py-exercise






NoteWorks on its own



py-exercise needs no Pyodide extension next to it. On its own it loads Pyodide and the editor from the network when the reader first runs an exercise:


exercises.qmd — standalone

filters:
  - Erasmus-CTM/py-exercise

If the page also has pyodide-interaktiv, list it first. py-exercise then reuses its Python instead of starting a second one:


page.qmd — combined

filters:
  - Erasmus-CTM/pyodide-interaktiv
  - Erasmus-CTM/py-exercise




ExampleSyntaxOptionsRestricting solutionsSubmission



  
    Please enable JavaScript to load the interactive exercise.
  




```{py-exercise}
def my_function(x):
    """Docstring shown to the reader."""
    # Student fills this in
    pass

## TESTS ##
assert my_function(2) == 4, "Feedback shown on failure"
assert my_function(0) == 0
```
Rules:

Write the function stub with a docstring at the top.
## TESTS ## is the separator. Everything below is hidden from the reader.
The text after the comma of an assert is the feedback shown when the test fails.







Tip



Write assertion messages as if you are talking to the student: "my_function(2) should return 4. Did you multiply correctly?"




Per exercise:








Option
Default
Description




label
py-exercise-N
unique exercise ID


caption
—
title above the exercise


forbidden-imports
—
comma-separated imports the solution may not use


forbidden-keywords
—
comma-separated keywords the solution may not use


show-test-hints
true
show the assertion message when a test fails



Per document, the same keys applied to every exercise on the page:


exercises.qmd

py-exercise:
  forbidden-imports: [os, sys, subprocess]
  forbidden-keywords: [for, while, sorted]
  show-test-hints: true
  lang: de                   # interface language (default: en)

The interface is available in German and English. Here too, Quarto’s own lang: is enough.


Forbidden constructs are checked before the code runs. A violation is reported instead of a test result:
```{py-exercise}
#| caption: Fibonacci, recursively
#| forbidden-keywords: for, while
def fib(n):
    pass

## TESTS ##
assert fib(6) == 8,   "fib(6) should be 8"
assert fib(10) == 55, "fib(10) should be 55"
```
Typical uses: banning for/while to force recursion or comprehensions, banning sorted to make students write the algorithm, banning os/sys/subprocess in an open learning environment.


With submission: true the page gets a header asking for a student ID and a quiz ID. Once the tests pass, the student can download the result as a JSON file, XOR-encoded with submission-key and Base64-wrapped so the results are not readable without the key.


exercises.qmd

py-exercise:
  submission: true
  submission-key: "sose25-quiz1"







Warning



The key is in the rendered page, so this deters casual tampering but is not real cryptography. Treat it as a convenience for collecting results, not as an exam-grade safeguard.

title: Extensions
text:
math-exercise — answers checked with SymPy
Install: quarto add Erasmus-CTM/math-exercise Source: (Erasmus CTM, n.d.a), github.com/Erasmus-CTM/math-exercise
Where py-exercise checks code, math-exercise checks an answer. Students type a mathematical expression into a field and SymPy compares it with the solution. In the default mode, any equivalent form therefore counts as correct.






NoteWorks on its own



Like py-exercise, math-exercise loads Pyodide and SymPy itself on the first Check click if no Pyodide extension is present. When one is, list it first:


page.qmd

filters:
  - Erasmus-CTM/pyodide-interaktiv
  - Erasmus-CTM/math-exercise




ExampleSyntaxOptionsCheck modesForm & partial creditQuestion poolsFeedback



Area of a circle


A circle has radius \(r = 3\). Give its area exactly (write pi for π):

\(A =\) 


  ✓ Check
  ⓘ Input help
  
    💬 Feedback
    ⚙
  





pi*9, 9*pi and 3**2*pi are all accepted; they are the same expression.


```{math-exercise}
#| label: my-exercise
#| caption: Exercise title
#| vars: x
Question text with an input field: _[correct_answer]
```
The answer inside [...] is a SymPy expression, e.g. pi * 9 or x**2 + 2*x + 1.



Marker
Field




_[answer]
narrow (about 10 characters)


__[answer]
medium (about 20 characters)


___[answer]
wide, two lines


vec[a,b,c]
bracketed vector, one field per component


mat[a,b;c,d]
bracketed matrix, one field per entry



Vector components are separated by commas. In matrices, commas separate columns and semicolons separate rows. Vectors are column vectors; #| vecdir: row makes them row vectors. Each component is checked and highlighted on its own.
```{math-exercise}
#| vars: x
Enter a vector: vec[x+1,2*x]
Enter a matrix: mat[1,0;0,x]
```
Several fields in one exercise are checked together on Check.






Important



Any symbol used in the answer has to be listed in vars. Otherwise SymPy does not know what x is meant to be.












Option
Default
Description




label
math-exercise-N
unique exercise ID


caption
—
title above the exercise


vars
—
SymPy symbols, e.g. x, y, r


mode
equivalent
check mode, see the “Check modes” tab


reject
—
expression to refuse even though it is correct (equivalent/exact only)


form
—
required representation: factored, expanded, single_fraction, lowest_terms (equivalent/exact only)


tolerance
—
numeric only: allowed deviation, absolute (0.5) or relative (5%)


decplaces
—
numeric only: round both sides to N decimal places before comparing


sigfigs
—
numeric only: round both sides to N significant figures before comparing


partial-credit
false
award partial credit


form-credit
0.5
score for an equivalent answer in the wrong representation


pool
false
treat the block as a pool of variants


vecdir
col
orientation of every vec[...]: col or row


field-labels
—
names of the fields, e.g. S, E, M


checker
—
your own checking code for mode: custom


packages
—
Pyodide packages for your own checker, e.g. networkx


response
—
take the answer from a JSXGraph board: jsxgraph:<assessment_id>


embed-response
false
move the board into the exercise card


context
—
context for AI feedback, see the “Feedback” tab





page.qmd

math-exercise:
  lang: de     # interface language (default: en)

The interface is available in English, German and Norwegian (Bokmål). Here too, Quarto’s own lang: is enough.


equivalent (default): accepts every mathematically equivalent form. For [pi * 9], all of pi*9, 9*pi and 3**2 * pi pass.
equivalent with reject: accepts equivalent forms except the one given. This is what makes simplification exercises work, where nobody should just retype the question.
```{math-exercise}
#| vars: x
#| reject: (x+1)**2
Expand: $(x+1)^2 =$ __[x**2 + 2*x + 1]
```
(x+1)^2 is refused, x^2 + 2x + 1 is accepted.
exact: the strictest mode, accepts only the one representation of the solution. Unreduced fractions are refused: for _[3/4], 3/4 is correct and 6/8 is not.
numeric: compares numeric values instead of expressions, for rounding and approximation tasks.
```{math-exercise}
#| mode: numeric
#| tolerance: 0.01
Approximate π: _[3.14159]
```
Everything that differs from \(3.14159\) by at most \(0.01\) is accepted: 3.14 and 3.15 are correct, 3.2 is not.
string and string_ci: compare the typed text literally, string_ci ignoring upper and lower case. For terms and units.
set: the answer is a comma-separated list; order does not matter.
```{math-exercise}
#| mode: set
Solve $x^2 = 4$. All solutions: __[2, -2]
```
-2, 2 and 2,-2 are correct. A missing or duplicate solution makes the answer wrong.
custom: you write the checking code yourself, as a function check(response, symbols). It returns True/False, a score from 0 to 1, or a dictionary with score and feedback.
```{math-exercise}
#| vars: x
#| mode: custom
#| checker: |
#|   def check(response, symbols):
#|       f = response["expressions"][0]
#|       x = symbols["x"]
#|       return simplify(diff(f, x) - 2*x) == 0

Give an antiderivative of $2x$: $F(x) =$ __[]
```
Here every function whose derivative is \(2x\) is correct, that is \(x^2 + c\) with any constant \(c\).






Warning



The checking code is in the rendered page and visible to students.




With form you require a specific representation in addition to correctness:



Value
Required form




factored
fully factored, e.g. (x+1)*(x+2)


expanded
fully expanded, e.g. x**2 + 3*x + 2


single_fraction
a single fraction instead of a sum of fractions


lowest_terms
a fully reduced fraction



```{math-exercise}
#| vars: x
#| form: factored
Factor $x^2 + 3x + 2$: __[(x+1)*(x+2)]
```
(x+1)*(x+2) is accepted. x**2 + 3*x + 2 is mathematically correct but not factored, and is reported as “correct, but not in factored form”.
Partial credit is switched on with partial-credit: true:

Several fields are averaged; empty fields count as zero.
For set the score is \(\frac{2M}{E + S}\), where \(M\) is the number of matched elements, \(E\) the number expected and \(S\) the number submitted. Missing and extra elements both lower the score.
An equivalent answer in the wrong representation receives form-credit.

Without the option, an answer is simply right or wrong.


With pool: true and --- as a separator, one block holds several variants. Each page visit picks one at random and keeps it for the session. The ↻ button loads a different one.
```{math-exercise}
#| label: circle-pool
#| caption: Area of a circle
#| pool: true
Radius r = 3 cm. $A =$ _[pi*9] cm²

---

Radius r = 5 cm. $A =$ _[pi*25] cm²

---

Radius r = 7 cm. $A =$ _[pi*49] cm²
```
All variants share the same options (vars, mode, reject).


Each exercise has a collapsible input help listing the notation students need: x^2 or x**2, sqrt(x), root(x, n), pi, E, Abs(x), oo, integrate(f, x), diff(f, x).
On the first click, the Feedback button opens the setup (provider, base URL, API key, model). The settings are stored in localStorage and apply to all pages of the project.
Hints get more concrete with each click. Unlike pyodide-interaktiv, there are four levels, and the fourth reveals the solution:







Click
Behaviour




1st
one question pointing toward the first likely mistake. No formula, no method, no intermediate value


2nd
a conceptual hint naming what to look at. No formulas, no calculation


3rd
guidance in at most three steps. A general formula is allowed; task values and the result stay hidden


4th and later
a concise complete worked solution with calculation and result



So that the AI understands the task correctly, it receives context:

Automatically: the text written since the last heading before the exercise (up to 1500 characters).
Explicitly: blocks with an id and the class .math-exercise-context, referenced by the exercise with #| context: id.
None at all: with #| context: none.

::: {#fp16 .math-exercise-context}
IEEE-754 half precision: 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits (bias 15),
10 mantissa bits.
:::

```{math-exercise}
#| label: fp-decode
#| context: fp16
Decode 0x3C00 as a half-precision float: _[1]
```






ImportantPrivacy



Clicking Feedback sends context, exercise text and the student’s answer to the configured provider. The expected answer is not sent.

title: Cheatsheet
Multilanguage Projects
text: Quarto does not have a built-in translation system, but profiles make it possible to build a project that serves several languages. This tutorial goes one step further: it has two axes, language (German, English, Swedish, Norwegian, Danish) and level (Beginner/Intermediate/Expert). Every combination is rendered into its own folder.

title: Multilanguage Projects
text:
The idea at a glance
                 beg                int                exp
deutsch   docs/de/beg/...    docs/de/int/...    docs/de/exp/...     + docs/de/index.html
english   docs/en/beg/...    docs/en/int/...    docs/en/exp/...     + docs/en/index.html
svenska   docs/sv/beg/...    docs/sv/int/...    docs/sv/exp/...     + docs/sv/index.html
norsk     docs/no/beg/...    docs/no/int/...    docs/no/exp/...     + docs/no/index.html
dansk     docs/da/beg/...    docs/da/int/...    docs/da/exp/...     + docs/da/index.html

One .qmd per page, all languages inside (see below).
The level profile (_quarto-beg.yml …) decides which pages are rendered.
The language profile (_quarto-english.yml …) decides what things are called: navbar, sidebars, lang.
A small script in the page ties it together: switching the language keeps the same page, switching the level goes to that level’s start page.

title: Multilanguage Projects
text:
Step 1 — Two profile groups


_quarto.yml

profile:
  default: [beg, deutsch]
  group:
    - [beg, int, exp, root]   # level (root = start page per language)
    - [deutsch, english, svenska, norsk, dansk]   # language

Exactly one profile of each group is active. Pass several profiles separated by commas:
quarto render --profile int,english --output-dir docs/en/int
Quarto then reads _quarto.yml, _quarto-int.yml and _quarto-english.yml and merges them.

title: Multilanguage Projects
text:
Step 2 — What goes where?


_quarto-int.yml

project:
  render:
    - "Qmd Files/Getting Started/*.qmd"



_quarto-english.yml (shortened)

lang: en
website:
  title: "Quarto Tutorial"
  navbar:
    left:
      - text: "Getting Started"
        href: "#niveau-int"          # placeholder, see step 4
    right:
      - icon: globe
        menu:
          - text: "Deutsch"
            href: "#sprache-de"
          - text: "English"
            href: "#sprache-en"
          # … Svenska, Norsk, Dansk
  sidebar:                            # sidebars of ALL levels
    - id: getting-started-sidebar
      contents:
        - text: "What you need"
          href: "Qmd Files/Getting Started/beg_website_1.qmd"
    - id: tips-sidebar
      ...

The sidebars of all levels live in the language file because their labels need translating. Quarto shows on each page only the sidebar that lists it. Entries for pages that are not rendered in this run do no harm.

title: Multilanguage Projects
section: Step 3 — All languages in one file
text:
Step 3 — All languages in one file
---
title: "Erste Schritte mit Quarto"
title-en: "Getting Started with Quarto"
---

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="deutsch"}
Willkommen! ...
::::

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="english"}
Welcome! ...
::::

The small filter sprache.lua turns title-en: (or title-sv:, title-no:, title-da:) into the title in the run for that language.
Content of the other languages is removed, not just hidden, so search only finds the current language.
Code cells in all blocks run in every run. If you compute something, write the code once outside the blocks and only translate the text around it.

title: Multilanguage Projects
text:
Step 4 — Navigation without post-processing
Quarto cannot link across profiles: from the point of view of the run int,english, docs/de/ or docs/en/beg/ do not exist. That is why preview.py used to rewrite every HTML file after rendering.
Now the navbar only contains placeholders (#sprache-de, #niveau-beg). The script navigation.html (added to every page via include-after-body) reads its own path, e.g. /en/int/Qmd Files/…, and fills in:



Placeholder
Target




#sprache-de
the same page, /en/ → /de/


#niveau-beg
Beginner start page in the current language


title top left
start page of the current language



Links in the text to a specific page of another level work without the script, as a relative path into the finished folder structure, e.g. ../../../int/Qmd Files/Getting Started/getting_started.html.

title: Multilanguage Projects
text:
Step 5 — Build everything
python build.py            # 5 languages × (start page + 3 levels) = 20 runs, then preview
python build.py --no-serve # build only
For each language the script first renders the start page (root), then the three levels into sub-folders, and writes docs/index.html, which redirects to the folder of the browser language (English if that language is missing).






WarningLimits




Search: every run has its own search index. Search only finds pages of the current level in the current language.
quarto preview shows a single combination; the placeholder links do nothing there.
Size: every page appears once per language in the same file. For very large projects separate folders per language are easier to maintain; the navigation from step 4 works the same way as long as file names match.

title: The YML File
text: The _quarto.yml file is the control centre of your Quarto project. Everything you set here applies globally, unless overridden in a specific .qmd file or profile.

title: The YML File
text:
Output formats
Quarto can render the same source to multiple formats at once:


_quarto.yml

format:
  html:
    toc: true
    theme: cosmo
  pdf:
    toc: true
    documentclass: article
  docx:
    toc: true

Run all formats: quarto render Run one format: quarto render --to pdf






Tip



Any format option can be overridden per page in the header of the .qmd file.

title: The YML File
text:
Execute & freeze


_quarto.yml

execute:
  echo: true        # show source code
  eval: true        # run the code
  warning: false    # suppress warnings
  freeze: auto      # re-run only when source changes




freeze value
Behaviour




false
Always re-execute


true
Never re-execute, use cached output


auto
Re-execute only when the .qmd file changes



Frozen results are stored in _freeze/. Commit this folder so collaborators don’t need to re-run everything.






Warning



freeze: auto watches the .qmd file, not your data files. If you update a CSV but not the .qmd, delete the matching folder in _freeze/ to force a re-run.

title: The YML File
text:
Profiles
Profiles let you maintain multiple build variants of one project, for different audiences, languages, or formats.


_quarto.yml

profile:
  default: web
  group:
    - [web, print]

Exactly one profile of a group is active at a time. Each profile has its own config file _quarto-<name>.yml that overrides or extends the root config:


_quarto-print.yml

project:
  output-dir: docs/print
format:
  pdf:
    toc: true

Render a specific profile:
quarto render --profile print






Tip



This tutorial has two groups of profiles: the level (beg, int, exp) and the language (deutsch, english, svenska, norsk, dansk). Every run has one of each group active, e.g. quarto render --profile int,english. More on this in Multilanguage Projects.

title: The YML File
text:
Sidebar

Basic setup


_quarto.yml

website:
  sidebar:
    - id: my-sidebar
      style: docked       # docked | floating
      collapse-level: 1   # how many levels are expanded by default
      contents:
        - href: page.qmd
          text: "Page Title"



Sections: collapsible groups
Use section: to create collapsible groups in the sidebar. A section can have its own overview page (href) or just be a label:
contents:
  - section: "Chapter 1"          # label only, no page
    contents:
      - href: ch1/part1.qmd
        text: Part 1

  - section: "Chapter 2"
    href: ch2/index.qmd           # clicking the section title opens this page
    contents:
      - href: ch2/part1.qmd
        text: Part 1


Collapse level
collapse-level controls how many nesting levels are expanded when the page loads:



Value
Effect




1
Only top-level items visible, all sections collapsed


2
First-level sections expanded (default)


3
Second-level sections expanded as well



sidebar:
  collapse-level: 1   # start collapsed, readers expand what they need


Docked or floating sidebar
style: docked shows the sidebar as a fixed column with its own background. style: floating places it next to the text without a background:
website:
  sidebar:
    style: floating
To hide the sidebar on a single page, use the header of that .qmd file:


page.qmd

---
sidebar: false
---

title: The YML File
